questions.q: Master data management (MDM) is primarily concerned with reconciling which kind of data across systems?
options: High-volume transactional data like orders and cases
Master data such as customers, products, and locations
Log and audit data
UI configuration metadata
questions.explain: MDM targets master data — the relatively stable, shared entities like customers, products, and locations — not transactional records, which are expected to be numerous and system-specific.

questions.q: Why does Salesforce's Data Cloud / Data 360 documentation describe its identity-resolution output as a 'Unified Profile' / 'system of reference' rather than a 'golden record'?
options: Because Salesforce does not support any form of record matching
Because the Unified Profile links source records together without overwriting or replacing the underlying source data
Because 'golden record' is a trademarked term owned by a competitor
Because Unified Profiles only apply to product data, never customer data
questions.explain: Salesforce's identity resolution links source profiles under match rules rather than overwriting them, so it avoids the 'golden record' framing, which implies one record replacing or superseding the others.

questions.q: A company has Salesforce, an ERP, and an e-commerce platform all able to independently edit the same customer data, with no clear single authority. Which hub-and-spoke pattern is designed for exactly this situation?
options: Registry / reference model only
Salesforce as master by default
A dedicated MDM hub that all three systems sync to and from
No pattern is needed since conflicts resolve automatically
questions.explain: A dedicated MDM hub fits organizations with three or more systems of comparable authority over the same entity, since no single operational system is positioned to be the master on its own.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a match rule and a survivorship rule in an MDM process?
options: A match rule decides which value wins after a conflict; a survivorship rule decides if two records are the same entity
A match rule decides if two records describe the same entity; a survivorship rule decides which field value wins once they're matched
They are two names for the same step
Match rules apply only to products; survivorship rules apply only to customers
questions.explain: Match rules identify that two records represent the same real-world entity; survivorship rules then decide, field by field, which of the matched records' values should be kept.

questions.q: Why might 'most recently updated wins' be a poor survivorship rule for a billing address field specifically?
options: Billing addresses never change, so the rule is irrelevant
A recent update could be a data-entry error, while an older value may have been verified through a signed contract
Salesforce does not store timestamps on address fields
Survivorship rules cannot be applied to address fields under any circumstances
questions.explain: Recency doesn't imply accuracy — a newer value could be an unverified mistake, while an older value might be backed by a more reliable source, which is why mature survivorship rules are field-by-field and source-aware.
